name: High-Temperature Aging: Extraction and Directed Mechanisms
description: Single-paper benchmark for evidence-grounded entity/relation extraction, directed causal reasoning, experimental conditions, quantitative facts and overclaim detection. Reference answers are grounded only in the supplied paper.
page_numbering: One-based physical PDF pages. Physical page 1 is printed page 44733; printed page = physical page + 44732.
evaluation_notes: Preserves the supplied top-level and case field structure. English questions and canonical concepts match the supplied fixture style.
All evidence is confined to the supplied paper. No results from other papers cited in its introduction are treated as this experiment.

Run extraction diagnostics before retrieval/path diagnostics. Noncausal cases deliberately have empty expected_directed_paths; skip path scoring for those cases, never treat empty paths as an automatic success.

Category-level macro averages are required: entity_extraction, relation_extraction, experimental_protocol, quantitative_fact, causal_chain, root_cause, synthesis and evidence_boundary. A runner may need support for new category names and empty paths; schema similarity alone does not establish runtime compatibility.

The inherited directed scorer does not establish entity mention-span/type F1, exact numerical accuracy, signed causality or hallucination rejection. Score expected_entities as concept recall; precision requires inspecting all extracted concepts against source evidence. Numeric and unacceptable_claims checks require a separate answer review.
Gold relation lists are selected diagnostic relations, not an exhaustive annotation of the paper. Do not label every additional supported edge a false positive.

Expected paths use at most three adjacent edges. Several cases query different windows of one mechanism: they are correlated, not independent experiments. Do not concatenate windows and claim evaluated five-hop accuracy.
In root-cause cases traversal_nodes run backward, but expected_relations retain cause-to-effect direction. Relation types on traversal paths follow traversal order.

The gas/drying/plating mechanism is the authors interpretation supported by post-mortem characterization, not an independently manipulated causal experiment; distinguish interpretation from directly measured observations.
Accepted relation aliases preserve the effect sign stated in expected_answer; generic influences is not sufficient to establish a signed increase/decrease.

Values are source-reported, not digitized from graphs. Preserve units, SOH, C-rate, electrode, temperature and measurement type. Table 2 overrides broad prose claims of universally increasing resistance.
Reversible heat is residual Qr=Q-Qi, not a separately measured chemical heat. Negative/endothermic contribution and magnitude must not be conflated with a signed numerical increase.
No evidence of thermal runaway thresholds, specific gas composition, direct gas quantification or universal applicability is supplied by these cases.
Fixed retrieval budget is inherited from the supplied fixture. Quality gates are provisional development targets, not validated scientific thresholds. Report category coverage alongside scores.

cases.question: How can electrolyte decomposition during high-temperature aging promote lithium plating on subsequent charging?

source_documents: Heat Generation and Degradation Mechanism of Lithium-Ion Batteries during High-Temperature Aging

cases.expected_answer: The proposed mechanism is decomposition -> gas -> altered electrode spacing and nonuniform local current -> plating during subsequent charging. Local drying is a parallel contributor. This is the authors mechanistic interpretation, not direct gas measurement.
unacceptable_claims: Gas generation alone proves an internal short circuit.
Lithium plating was measured during the 60 °C discharge itself.

evidence.support: Decomposition produces gas; spacing and drying affect current distribution; plating occurs on subsequent charging.

cases.expected_answer: Capacity calibration at 25 °C; cyclic aging at 60 °C; adiabatic discharge starts at 30 °C after 90 min calibration and its temperature then rises. Aging temperature is not discharge-test temperature.

cases.question: Compare standard capacity testing and high-temperature cyclic aging in Table 1.
cases.expected_answer: Standard: CC charge 1.4 A to 4.2 V, CV at 4.2 V to 0.021 A, rest 30 min, CC discharge 1.4 A to 2.5 V, rest 30 min; repeat three times and use last discharge capacity. Aging: same voltage/rest/CV cutoffs but CC charge/discharge 2.1 A, blocks of 20 cycles, followed by calibration at 25 °C.
unacceptable_claims: The aging discharge current is 1.4 A.

evidence.support: Table 1 plus surrounding methods defines both protocols.

cases.expected_answer: EIS at 100%, 95%, 90% SOH on fully charged cells; sinusoidal current amplitude 0.1 A; frequency range 0.01–10 kHz as printed (upper endpoint 10 kHz). Electrochemical tests at 25 °C. Do not confuse AC amplitude with the 2.1 A HPPC pulse.
unacceptable_claims: The EIS amplitude is 2.1 A.

evidence.support: EIS protocol states checkpoints, charge state, amplitude and frequency range.

cases.question: How is internal resistance obtained from HPPC and combined from charge/discharge pulses?
cases.expected_answer: At 25 °C: fully charged cell rests 1 h; 2.1 A charge pulse 10 s, rest 60 s, 2.1 A discharge pulse 10 s; reduce SOC by 10% with 1.4 A discharge, rest 1 h, repeat to zero SOC. R uses the average of charge and discharge pulse resistances Rc and Rd, each based on voltage change/current.

evidence.support: Pulse timing, current and SOC steps.

evidence.anchor: taken as the internal resistance of the cell

cases.expected_answer: ΔT in °C; columns 0.25 C / 0.33 C / 0.5 C: 100% SOH 28.7/32/42.4; 95% 24.2/30.8/40.3; 90% 31.4/34/47.8. These are temperature rises, not absolute final temperatures.

cases.question: Explain why temperature rise first decreases and then increases with aging despite continuous capacity fading.
cases.expected_answer: At 95% SOH the rise rate differs little from fresh, while lower capacity reduces total discharge duration and temperature rise. At 90% severe degradation raises the heating rate enough to dominate capacity loss, so total rise exceeds fresh. At 0.5 C the measured rises are 42.4, 40.3, 47.8 °C for 100, 95, 90% SOH. Do not infer unchanged capacity from higher heating.
unacceptable_claims: All aged cells show less temperature rise than fresh.
All aged cells show more temperature rise than fresh.

evidence.support: The discussion distinguishes early capacity-dominated from later rate-dominated heating.

cases.question: Give specific heat capacity at the three SOHs and its role in calorimetry.
cases.expected_answer: Cp at 100/95/90% SOH is 1.1352/1.1522/1.2087 J/(g·°C), respectively. Equation 7 uses Q=Cp M ΔT. Do not assume the same Cp across SOHs or compare heat solely using ΔT.

evidence.support: The paragraph gives all Cp values; Equation 7 relates them to heat.

cases.question: How are total, irreversible and reversible heat obtained and related?
cases.expected_answer: Q=Qr+Qi; Q from ARC temperature rise via Cp M ΔT. Qi=I²Rt uses internal resistance from HPPC; Qr=Q−Qi is the residual. For time-varying R the printed expression must be applied appropriately over intervals; no separately measured entropic coefficient is reported.
unacceptable_claims: Reversible heat was independently directly measured by XPS.

evidence.anchor: heat generated by the cell is mainly composed of two parts
evidence.support: Heat balance.

evidence.anchor: reversible heat of the cell can be obtained
evidence.support: Equations 5–7 and HPPC attribution.

expected_documents: Heat Generation and Degradation Mechanism of Lithium-Ion Batteries during High-Temperature Aging
cases.question: Can total released heat be smaller than irreversible heat in this paper, and what does that imply?
cases.expected_answer: Yes. Section 3.2 describes endothermic internal reactions offsetting part of irreversible heat, so Q can be lower than Qi. With Q=Qr+Qi, the corresponding Qr contribution is negative. Wording that reversible heat increases must distinguish magnitude from algebraic sign; do not assume all reversible contributions are exothermic.
unacceptable_claims: Total heat must always exceed irreversible heat.
Reversible heat is always exothermic.

evidence.support: The paragraph states endothermic offset and total heat lower than irreversible heat.

evidence.anchor: heat generated by the cell is mainly composed of two parts
evidence.support: Heat balance supports the signed interpretation.

cases.question: How does DC resistance vary with SOC, and where is its minimum?
cases.expected_answer: During discharge resistance first decreases with declining SOC, reaches a minimum around 40% SOC, then increases. Aging raises resistance and makes this nonmonotonic SOC dependence more pronounced. This is not a minimum at 40% SOH.
unacceptable_claims: Resistance decreases monotonically down to zero SOC.

evidence.support: Text explicitly locates resistance minimum and describes SOC dependence.

unacceptable_claims: LiF is assigned to 687.1 eV.

evidence.support: All binding energies and assignments are listed in the XPS paragraph.

cases.question: What differences did EDS show between fresh and aged anodes, and how are they interpreted?
cases.expected_answer: Carbon dominates fresh anode. Relative carbon content is lower and oxygen content higher on the aged anode; authors attribute this to oxygen-rich products coating graphite after electrolyte/plated-lithium side reactions. Relative surface elemental signals are not proof of a measured bulk carbon mass loss.
unacceptable_claims: EDS proves bulk graphite mass loss quantitatively.

evidence.anchor: carbon content in the aged anode
evidence.support: Direct EDS observations and subsequent reaction-product interpretation.

Do not identify particular dissolved metals or amounts that are not specified.
unacceptable_claims: The cathode remains entirely chemically unchanged.

evidence.support: Cathode comparison and transition metals detected on the anode are discussed together.

cases.question: Compare two distinct routes by which electrolyte degradation contributes to SEI thickening.

source_documents: Heat Generation and Degradation Mechanism of Lithium-Ion Batteries during High-Temperature Aging
Heat Generation and Degradation Mechanism of Lithium-Ion Batteries during High-Temperature Aging

cases.expected_answer: Route A: decomposition produces gas/drying, nonuniform recharge current and plating; plated lithium reacts with electrolyte and thickens SEI. Route B: electrolyte decomposition products also directly contribute to SEI thickening. They converge at SEI growth; do not assert that all SEI growth requires plating.
